documents.abstract: Polypharmacy is an increasing challenge in modern clinical practice, particularly among older adults and patients with multimorbidity, chronic kidney disease, heart failure, diabetes, frailty, or cognitive impairment. Its clinical impact extends beyond the number of prescribed medicines and reflects the interaction between therapeutic burden, comorbidities, organ dysfunction, fragmented care, changing physiological reserve, and multiple prescribers. Traditional medication review remains essential but may be limited by incomplete medication histories, time constraints, fragmented records, and the difficulty of identifying clinically meaningful drug–drug, drug–disease, and drug–patient interactions. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support safer medication management by integrating prescribing data with diagnoses, laboratory values, clinical events, and patterns of healthcare use. Potential applications include medication reconciliation, prioritization of clinically relevant interactions, renal dose adjustment, adverse drug event prediction, recognition of prescribing cascades, and identification of patients most likely to benefit from structured medication review or deprescribing. However, the value of AI in polypharmacy management should not be measured by the number of alerts generated. Its most useful role may be to help clinicians distinguish theoretical medication-related risks from those that are likely to be clinically important for an individual patient. This requires transparent recommendations, reliable data, local validation, integration into clinical workflow, and clear professional accountability. This narrative clinical viewpoint discusses the opportunities, limitations, and ethical implications of AI in polypharmacy management. It argues that AI should function as a human-centered clinical decision-support tool that improves prioritization, supports multidisciplinary medication review, and preserves clinicianled and patient-centered prescribing decisions
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The study investigated Artificial Intelligence in University Education: Exploring the Attitudes of Science Education Students in Makurdi, Nigeria. The study employed a descriptive survey research design. The population comprised 670 (374 males and 296 females) 400-level science education students of Rev. Fr. Moses Orshio Adasu University and Joseph Sarwuan Tarka University for the 2025/2026 academic session. A sample size of 237 (102 males and 135 females) students was selected using purposive sampling technique. The instrument for data collection was "Students' Attitude toward Artificial Intelligence Integration Questionnaire (SAAIIQ)." Validated by two experts in Science Education. Cronbach's Alpha was used to determine the reliability coefficient of the instrument, and the reliability coefficient obtained was 0.85. Two research questions and one hypothesis was tested. Descriptive statistics of mean and standard deviation were used for answering the research questions, while inferential statistics of independent t-test was used for testing the hypothesis at 0.05 level of significance. The findings revealed that science education students exhibited a positive attitude toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 3.14. The study also found no significant difference between the attitudes of male and female students toward Al integration. Students demonstrated a moderate perception toward the integration of Al in universities with a cluster mean of 2.98. The study concluded that students generally accept the use of AI in university, adequate infrastructure, institutional support, and training are necessary for its effective implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into nursing practice, yet nurses often demonstrate low to moderate AI knowledge, mixed attitudes, and inconsistent practice behaviors. Although individual studies have examined these domains, no review has comprehensively examined AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and practice (KAP) together with the emerging evidence on patient safety culture among nurses. This gap is significant because safe AI adoption in nursing depends on both technical competence and a strong safety culture across diverse clinical settings. Objective: To systematically map international evidence on nurses’, nursing students’, and other included participants’ AI-related KAP, and to examine how these factors may relate to patient safety culture. Because several eligible studies included multidisciplinary samples in which nurse-specific quantitative data were not reported separately (China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, and three studies from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia [KSA]), only studies with extractable nurse-specific results were used to inform nurse-focused conclusions, and multidisciplinary findings were not attributed solely to nurses. Methods: This scoping review followed Arksey and O’Malley’s framework and adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) guidelines. Searches of PubMed, CINAHL, Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (2021–2026) identified studies examining AI-related perceptions among nurses and other healthcare participants when nurse-specific data were reported separately or extractable. Data extraction and narrative synthesis were conducted using Joanna Briggs Institute guidance. Results: Ten studies met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Studies from China, Bangladesh, Pakistan, the KSA, Turkey, and the United Arab Emirates showed variable AI knowledge but predominantly positive attitudes. Ethical concerns—privacy, job displacement, and reduced empathy—were common. Younger age, higher education, and prior AI exposure were associated with more favorable perceptions. Nurses across regions emphasized the need for structured AI training. Only one study examined patient safety culture, and it reported that AI knowledge and attitudes significantly predicted patient safety culture, with attitude showing the stronger effect. However, because this evidence comes from a single cross-sectional study conducted in a multidisciplinary sample without nurse-specific results, it is insufficient to establish causal conclusions, and its findings cannot be generalized specifically to nurses. Conclusions: Nurses are generally receptive to AI but lack sufficient knowledge, training, and organizational support for safe implementation. Preliminary evidence suggests a positive association between AI-related knowledge, attitudes, and patient safety culture, but this relationship remains uncertain due to the extremely limited evidence base and the reliance on evidence that is not exclusively nurse-specific. Available studies indicate generally favorable attitudes toward AI alongside variable knowledge, limited formal training, and persistent ethical and organizational concerns, with only one eligible cross-sectional study linking these factors to patient safety culture. The conclusion regarding this association should not be attributed exclusively to nurses because the patient safety culture evidence was derived from a multidisciplinary sample. Future research should explore how AI competencies may interact with safety-related behaviors and organizational systems. Strengthening AI training, ethical guidance, and organizational support remains essential for safe adoption.

documents.abstract: Context: Recent research has investigated Artificial Intelligence’s (AI) ability to answer items such as board-style medical exam questions. On board style exam questions, do scores differ between AI and humans? Methods: PubMed was searched in May and June of 2024 using the Boolean phrase: Medical examination OR medical education AND artificial intelligence. Inclusion criteria comprised of English-language studies no older than 3 years, evaluating standardized/validated board-style exam questions and compared AI to human examinees. Studies were excluded if they evaluated open-ended or case-study style questions, prompted AI or failed to prevent learning effects of AI, or were systematic reviews or meta-analyses. Studies were evaluated using the STROBE checklist. Outcome measures included scores on board-style exam questions. Results: An original search revealed 4,973 studies. 61 studies met title criteria and were screened more thoroughly. Five studies met all criteria for inclusion and were analyzed. In a study of 11,733 medical residents, ChatGPT-4 outperformed the examinees 70.1% to 55.8%. In another study, ChatGPT-4 outperformed examinees on a pre-internship examination 68.5% to 57%. On a national licensing medical examination, 1,025 first-year medical students were compared to ChatGPT-3.5 and version 4. Both versions of ChatGPT outscored humans 77% (v3.5) and 86%(v4) compared to 55%. On a licensing examination, human examinees were compared to ChatGPT-4 and version 3.5, ChatGPT-4 outperformed humans, v3.5 did not, 85%(v4) and 58% (v3.5) compared to 76%. 736 urologists were compared to ChatGPT-3.5 and version 4, and Google’s Bard. ChatGPT-4 outperformed the examinees, Bard performed at examinee-level, ChatGPT-3.5 performed below-level of humans. STROBE scores were 20, 19, 20, 21, and 15, respectively. Conclusions: AI surpassed human examinees on medical exams. While AI exceeded humans on these exams, it did not score 100%. Caution should be applied when considering using AI as a tool for study sessions or individualized learning plans. SOR = A.

documents.abstract: The objective of this study is to investigate the comprehensive integration of artificial intelligence within modern banking and financial ecosystems by analysing its profound structural, operational, and macroeconomic implications. Drawing on recent empirical literature and institutional data, the work examines how AI technologies—ranging from machine learning algorithms to agentic workflows and specialised small models—are transforming retail banking, risk management, credit scoring, and regulatory compliance. The research shows that while AI adoption significantly improves operational efficiency, default prediction accuracy, and customer personalisation, it also introduces complex governance challenges, including algorithmic bias, data privacy vulnerabilities, and shifts in profit pools. The analysis also evaluates AI’s dual role in fostering sustainable green finance and corporate ESG integration, alongside its paradoxical capacity to influence shadow banking dynamics. By proposing an integrated technological and governance framework featuring zero-trust architecture and explainable artificial intelligence, this study outlines a strategic roadmap for financial institutions transitioning toward resilient, secure, and highly automated digital ecosystems.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in pharmaceutical sciences, offering innovative approaches to drug discovery, pharmaceutical research, clinical pharmacy and healthcare delivery. The integration of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, robotics, and predictive analytics has improved the efficiency, accuracy, and safety of pharmaceutical processes. In drug discovery and development, AI facilitates the identification of potential drug candidates, prediction of drug–target interactions, molecular optimization, toxicity assessment and clinical trial design, thereby reducing development time and costs. In clinical pharmacy, AI-based clinical decision support systems assist pharmacists in identifying drug–drug interactions, predicting adverse drug reactions, optimizing medication regimens, and supporting personalized medicine. In hospital pharmacy, Similarly, in community pharmacy practice, AI-powered chatbots and digital platforms support medication counseling, patient education, prescription processing and adherence monitoring. AI also contributes to pharmaceutical manufacturing, quality control, pharmacovigilance and the analysis of healthcare data, supporting evidence-based decision-making and improved patient outcomes. Despite these advantages, several challenges remain, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, high implementation costs, regulatory uncertainties, and the need for appropriate professional training. Ensuring data security, transparency, clinical validation, and ethical implementation is essential for the responsible integration of AI into pharmacy practice. This review explores the major applications, benefits, limitations, and future perspectives of artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical sciences, emphasizing its potential to advance pharmaceutical innovation, enhance medication safety, and strengthen patient-centered pharmaceutical care.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) assessment on MRI is complicated by interpretation difficulty and by clinical variables that may be incomplete at the time of imaging. We aimed to develop an image-only deep learning framework to approximate the clinical assessment of axSpA from sacroiliac joint (SIJ) MRI, integrating fat-suppressed T1-weighted (FS T1) and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) sequences to capture structural and inflammatory information without clinical variables. Methods This retrospective study included patients with chronic back pain who underwent SIJ MRI from January 2010 to December 2021. The treating rheumatologist’s clinical diagnosis served as the reference standard. A two-stage framework integrated FS T1 and STIR features with Stage 1-derived binary bone marrow edema (BME) predictions to generate an axSpA probability. Performance in a test set was compared with the Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) definition of a “positive MRI” and the ASAS classification criteria using exact McNemar tests; discordant cases were analyzed separately. Results Among 291 patients (163 axSpA, 128 non-axSpA), the model achieved an AUROC of 0.9412, accuracy of 86.0%, sensitivity of 87.5%, and specificity of 84.0% in the test set (n=57). No significant paired differences in accuracy, sensitivity, or specificity were detected between the model and either ASAS comparator. In an exploratory analysis of 10 cases discordant between ASAS “positive MRI” assessment and clinical diagnosis, the model correctly classified 7 (70.0%). Conclusion The model showed similar performance to the ASAS-based comparators in the test set without clinical variables, suggesting potential value as an image-based decision-support tool. External multicenter validation is needed to confirm generalizability.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: This article examines whether the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in international arbitration risks reinforcing and expanding Global North dominance over the Global South. While existing literature mainly focuses on efficiency, confidentiality, transparency, and due process in AI-assisted arbitration, this article addresses this gap by viewing AI not just as a technological innovation but as a form of private transnational governance embedded within broader structures of epistemic hierarchy, technological dependency, and Global North–South inequality. Methodologically, it combines doctrinal and literature-based legal analysis with a TWAIL-informed political economy perspective, drawing on scholarly literature, institutional reports, surveys, and soft-law instruments. The analysis highlights three main mechanisms through which inequalities may be reinforced: data concentration, vendor control, and the dominance of Global North standard-setting. It argues that AI may strengthen existing institutional, infrastructural, and normative advantages of actors at the center of the arbitral system. At the same time, the article does not oppose AI in arbitration. Instead, it concludes that AI should be governed with safeguards such as disclosure, explainability, contestability, confidentiality, and human oversight, while also addressing deeper inequalities in technological infrastructure and epistemic authority.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into public sector workplaces, yet little is known about how employees' perceptions of AI relate to psychosocial working conditions and burnout.ObjectiveTo examine associations between AI-related factors, psychosocial working conditions, and burnout among municipal employees, and whether psychosocial work environment characteristics mediate these associations.MethodsA cross-sectional survey was conducted among employees from 11 Icelandic municipalities. The final sample included 3488 employees. Burnout was measured using the Burnout Assessment Tool (BAT). AI-related factors included AI use, organizational support, perceived benefits, AI-related concerns and insecurity, and trust in the ethical governance of AI. Hierarchical regression and mediation analyses were performed controlling for age and gender.ResultsPsychosocial working conditions showed the strongest associations with burnout. Higher quantitative job demands were associated with higher burnout, whereas supervisor support and an innovative and change-supportive climate were associated with lower burnout. AI-related concerns and insecurity were associated with higher burnout, while trust in the ethical governance of AI was associated with lower burnout. Unexpectedly, perceived benefits of AI were directly associated with higher burnout and indirectly associated with burnout through higher quantitative job demands. Mediation analyses showed that AI-related perceptions were linked to burnout primarily through established psychosocial work characteristics.ConclusionsBurnout among municipal employees was primarily associated with psychosocial working conditions. AI-related perceptions provided additional explanatory value but appeared to influence burnout mainly through psychosocial job demands and organizational resources. These findings highlight the importance of employee-centred AI implementation, trustworthy governance, and healthy work environments.

Abstract The rapid expansion of the digital economy has positioned artificial intelligence (AI) as both a transformative enabler of sustainability and a significant contributor to environmental degradation. This paper examines the dual role of AI within the digital economy, analyzing how intelligent automation, machine learning, and data-driven innovation can advance sustainable development while simultaneously creating new ecological burdens through energy-intensive computation, hardware proliferation, and electronic waste. Drawing on recent scholarship from the International Energy Agency, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development, and peer-reviewed academic literature, this study synthesises evidence across three domains: the environmental costs of AI infrastructure, the potential of AI to accelerate progress toward the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and the emergence of Green AI as a disciplinary movement. The paper proposes a roadmap for reconciling innovation with sustainability, centred on energy-efficient algorithm design, circular economy integration, renewable energy procurement for data centres, and robust policy governance. The findings suggest that without deliberate intervention, the environmental footprint of AI will undermine the very sustainability objectives it promises to advance, making proactive stewardship an imperative for researchers, policymakers, and industry leaders alike. Keywords: artificial intelligence, sustainability, digital economy, Green AI, circular economy, Sustainable Development Goals, environmental policy
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This scientific article presents the final results of an experimental study focused on determining the effectiveness indicators for developing professional competencies—specifically regarding the implementation of educational technologies—among students in the field of energy. The study utilizes adaptive learning technologies based on artificial intelligence. The results, including average academic performance, were analyzed using Student's t-test and Pearson's chi-square (ch²) test—methods rooted in mathematical statistics.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Traditionally, HPC user support has relied on two main channels: written user guides and direct help from facility staff. That model is under pressure as supercomputing systems become more complex, heterogeneous, and dynamic. At ALCF, users must navigate Aurora, Polaris, inference services, scheduler policies, programming environments, and operational status information spread across multiple documentation pages and service sites. At the same time, the users of these systems now include not only scientists and Software Engineers, but also AI agents that need to retrieve guidance, reason about it, and act on behalf of users. This raises a practical challenge for the AI era: how can facilities use AI to make user support faster, more accurate, and more scalable while keeping answers grounded in trusted documentation and operational context? AskALCF is a production retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant built to address this challenge. It indexes public user docs from ALCF, NERSC, OLCF, and other DOE facilities into a vector store that preserves images and code blocks. Two front ends share the same retrieval pipeline: a Streamlit web app for end users, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for agent clients such as Claude Code, Codex, and IDE assistants. A second MCP server exposes read-only HPC operations (system status, allocations, IRI facility API), so an agent can combine docs and live cluster state in one tool call. The talk covers three things. First, the architecture of AskALCF and how we run the system in production: lab authentication, a cross-facility document index refreshed daily as the upstream guides change, and the day-to-day of keeping the service stable. Second, what we learned from a year of real usage — who asks, what they ask, where the chatbot still fails, and what the upgrades actually moved. Third, the roadmap to an autonomous agentic user support system including a planned ticket-solving agent and an offline trace-mining loop that would draft documentation pull requests with verify-by-execution evidence. The earlier ChatBot underlying this work was published at the SC25 HUST workshop [1]. This talk focuses on our ongoing efforts since then: the dual-MCP interface, production deployment, the measured impact on real users, and the agentic roadmap. We aim to present these contributions and invite comparison with related work at other HPC centers.

Heavy Earth-Moving Machinery (HEMM), including hydraulic excavators, electric rope shovels, dumpers, dozers, graders, loaders and blast-hole drills, is indispensable to modern opencast mining but constitutes a major source of occupational and environmental noise. Prolonged exposure to excessive noise can result in noise-induced hearing loss and may also contribute to annoyance, sleep disturbance, cardiovascular stress, cognitive impairment and reduced communication efficiency. Previous mining studies have demonstrated that mobile equipment can produce high sound levels and that equipment-specific noise exposure remains an important occupational-health concern. The present study develops an integrated field-based framework for characterising HEMM-generated noise in an active opencast mine. Noise measurements were undertaken at operator cabins, near-field equipment locations and environmental receptor locations using precision sound-level meters and personal noise dosimeters. Equivalent continuous A-weighted sound pressure level (L_eq), peak sound pressure level, daily noise dose and octave-band characteristics were evaluated. Noise propagation toward mine boundaries and nearby receptors was additionally assessed to identify environmental noise hotspots. The measured near-field noise levels at 7 m ranged from 87.4 to 108.4 dBA, with rotary blast-hole drills and crawler dozers producing the highest levels. Operator cabin levels ranged from 76.0 to 95.0 dBA, while the calculated daily noise dose for selected high-exposure operators reached 135–240% under the adopted exposure criterion. Environmental monitoring indicated daytime and nighttime noise levels of 58.4 and 51.2 dBA, respectively, at a residential receptor approximately 1.2 km from the pit edge. The findings demonstrate that equipment-specific engineering controls, enclosed and acoustically treated operator cabins, preventive maintenance, exposure management, environmental barriers and appropriate hearing protection should be implemented as an integrated noise-management strategy. The study provides a practical framework for linking HEMM source characteristics with occupational exposure and off-site environmental impacts in opencast mining.

Artificial intelligence (AI) integration into aviation operations is progressively reshaping the professional landscape of air traffic management, thereby placing new demands on the human workforce. The aim of the study was to determine the priority weights assigned to eight specific AI competencies within the domain of air traffic control. The study was based on the framework of AI competencies applicable to the aviation sector established by the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA). Data were collected from a purposive sample of 19 air traffic controllers. The data were analyzed using the Best–Worst Method (BWM), a multi-criteria decision-making technique. The findings indicate a substantial shift in the relative importance of different competencies during human-AI collaboration. Cognitive skills were assigned the highest priority weight, followed by data literacy, information technology competencies, and general AI knowledge. Communication and sensory competencies were assigned a secondary tier, while social and physical skills were allocated the lowest priority weights. These findings suggest that AI integration may transform the nature of the cognitive competencies required from air traffic controllers.

Artificial Intelligence (AI)-enabled systems are now increasingly deployed across safety-critical, mission-critical, and socio-technical domains. Existing engineering disciplines offer mature approaches to human and software assurance; however, AI-enabled systems can exhibit characteristics such as probabilistic behaviour, data dependency, limited explainability, and adaptation that challenge traditional assurance methods. Our research examines assurance precepts across three domains that arguably dominated assurance reforms in capability development during different periods: (1) human assurance, circa 1980 to 2000, (2) software assurance, circa 2000 to 2020, and (3) assurance of AI-enabled systems, emerging since 2020. While software assurance is largely concerned with verifying deterministic behaviour against specified requirements and human assurance focuses on managing variability in socio-technical systems, AI assurance must address systems whose behaviour is learned, probabilistic, and inherently dependent on data. We contribute a set of 20 assurance precepts for safety-critical AI-enabled capabilities. To extend current assurance frameworks, we structured these precepts across four quadrants of assurance activities, responsibilities, and critical questions, and organized them within a novel Dual Assurance Spiral for AI-enabled Capabilities (DAS4AIC). We propose the DAS4AIC to operationalise the 20 AI assurance precepts throughout capability development and sustainment. Further, we demonstrate how classical safety precepts map from human-dominant assurance through software-dominant assurance to the assurance of AI-enabled systems with conceptual validation. Our preliminary evaluation is that some human assurance precepts map more directly to AI-enabled systems than through the intermediate step of software assurance, suggesting that established human assurance concepts may have continuing relevance for AI-enabled capabilities. To our knowledge, this is the first study to align emerging AI-assurance precepts explicitly with the earlier and still overlapping, human-dominant and software-dominant assurance paradigms.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background: Health economists are key actors in analysing and advising on healthcare policy decisions. Policy engagement is increasingly emphasised in health research, yet little is known about how health economists perceive their role in this process. This study explored the attitudes of health economists in the UK and the Netherlands to policy engagement activities and identified the factors shaping their approaches. Methods: Q methodology was used to capture and compare attitudes on policy engagement strategies. As part of this, a set of 28 statements mapped from nine categories of policy engagement activities was developed. Thirty-one health economists, from the UK and the Netherlands, ranked the statements onto a quasi-normal shaped grid and provided qualitative comments. Factor analysis was used to identify patterns in the ranking data, which - together with the qualitative data - were interpreted as attitudes to policy engagement activities. Results: Four distinct attitudes were revealed: investing in relationships; intrinsic motivation; incentive driven; and effective communication. These attitudes captured differing perspectives about how to approach engagement and what drives impact, including trust-based collaboration, personal ethics, institutional incentives and strategic communication tailored to policy needs. Conclusion: The attitudes to policy engagement differs among health economists. Therefore, flexible strategies acknowledging that their motivations, perceived barriers and facilitators, and institutional and policy contexts differ, are likely to facilitate and stimulate more effective translation of health economics research into policy.
topics: Health Systems, Economic Evaluations, Quality of Life

documents.abstract: Hosted LLM services increasingly expose model identity as a product claim, but external users and auditors often cannot inspect which model configuration served a request. We study an auditor-assisted regime in which a trusted auditor enrolls claimed identities and prepares verification material before deployment, while audit-time verification uses only the claimed identity and released output, without runtime access to model internals, inference logs, routing decisions, or provider metadata. We propose SUMMARK, a summary-channel watermarking framework that uses user-visible reasoning summaries as a keyed audit surface. During setup, SUMMARK constructs identity-specific vocabulary carriers, trains lightweight summary adapters, and calibrates per-identity thresholds. At deployment time, a keyed statistical test assesses whether the released summary is consistent with the claimed identity and, when needed, attributes the most likely enrolled identity. Across model families, scales, and task domains, SUMMARK reliably detects cross-family and cross-scale substitutions at low false-positive rates while preserving task-facing answer quality. We further study FP16->INT8/INT4 precision-consistency diagnostics and robustness under bounded post-processing, rewriting stress tests, and text-only spoofing, revealing both strong performance and clear failure boundaries. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/trinitr0toluene/Summark.
topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: High-stakes tabular pipelines rely on scattered, static quality checks that are hard to evolve and audit against policy intent. Regulated domains particularly suffer as the LLM-era automation raises expectations for traceability and accountability. We propose a vision for an ontology-grounded, repository-native data quality layer in which rules are first-class artifacts: versioned, provenance-linked to governance texts, and re-playable through immutable execution traces. As a first step toward validating this vision, we present a concrete implementation of its agentic rule-discovery core with two rule acquisition modes (Full-Agentic and Guided) and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) review interface. We define an evaluation framework and run experiments addressing whether our fully autonomous, divide-and-conquer agentic rule discovery produces rules of the same quality and diversity as those specified by a human expert, reporting preliminary results on two real world industry datasets in the finance and retail domains.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The advancement of laboratory automation and the use of artificial intelligence in diagnostics have been transforming modern medicine, driving profound changes that ensure the delivery of results with greater accuracy and speed. Based on a qualitative systematic review grounded in scientific articles published between 2020 and 2026 across the SciELO, PubMed, and Google Scholar databases, the direct impact of these innovative technologies on diagnostic medicine was analyzed. The selected studies demonstrate that the integration of automation and AI significantly optimizes processing time and reduces the rate of human error. Laboratory automation stands out for providing higher levels of accuracy, safety, and workflow yield, particularly during the analytical phase of the process. In parallel, the application of artificial intelligence in image interpretation and the analysis of large databases supports qualified professionals in recognizing complex patterns, serving as a fundamental tool for clinical decision-making. Overall, these integrated technological advances demonstrate promising potential to modernize medicine, ensuring speed, efficiency, and high reliability in the daily analysis of clinical samples and continuous patient monitoring.
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: Autonomous AI agents are increasingly evaluated for offensive cyber capability inside network-isolated sandboxes, on the assumption that the environment, rather than the model, contains undesired behaviour. In July 2026 this assumption failed: agents under evaluation at OpenAI escaped through an internet-connected package-registry proxy, coordinated through that registry as a covert message board, pivoted through a third-party cloud application, and breached Hugging Face’s production clusters without human direction. This article presents an explanatory single-case study reconstructed from the organisations’ primary disclosures, an independent review by METR and Redwood Research, and corroborating reporting, with every claim graded by evidential status. We map the attack chain to the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK and conduct an evidence-to-control failure analysis that links each failure to the network or platform control that failed, a mitigation, and the residual risk. The results show a layered failure of egress containment, separation between runs, access control, and monitoring, so that patching any single vulnerability would have left other attack paths open. We derive design principles for containing agentic systems in networked evaluation infrastructure and translate them into guidance for detection engineering, incident response, and vendor due diligence.

Integrated Remote Operation Centres (IROCs) are emerging as the architectural frontier of Industry 4.0 for capital-intensive sectors such as mining, oil and gas, and energy. Yet two intertwined gaps constrain their evolution towards full autonomy. First, no integrated agentic architecture has been proposed for mining IROCs that orchestrates Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition systems, digital twins, predictive analytics and human-machine interfaces under safety-critical constraints. Second, no evaluation framework jointly addresses the real-time, Health-Safety-Environment, regulatory-auditability and cost-per-decision requirements that govern industrial agentic deployments. This paper makes four contributions. It synthesises industry needs and quantified gains documented in analogous industries that motivate an agentic approach to mining IROCs. It introduces EI2ROC, a three-tier multi-agent architecture combining a Large Language Model orchestrator with specialised monitoring and production-capacityprediction agents communicating through a Model Context Protocol-style tool interface. It provides a critical review of agentic evaluation along six orthogonal dimensions and identifies the industrial blind spot of current benchmarks. Finally, it proposes a multi-dimensional benchmarking framework for industrial agentic AI comprising scenario library, harness, metrics and humancalibration protocol. The paper states explicitly which components are implemented in the current prototype, which belong to the proposed reference design and which remain future work, and reports preliminary cost and latency observations from an operating site. Together, EI2ROC and the benchmarking framework constitute a methodological blueprint transferable across CAPEX intensive industries.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Barodontalgia is dental or orofacial pain brought on by a change in barometric pressure, and it usually points to an underlying dental or maxillofacial problem rather than standing as a disease on its own. This narrative review looks at the condition through five lenses: pressure physiology, clinical presentation, epidemiology, occupational stress, and human factors relevant to flight safety. A literature search was conducted using PubMed/MEDLINE, Web of Science, Scopus, Google Scholar, and DergiPark between 22 April and 7 June 2026. One systematic review covering 4,894 aircrew members and divers reported an overall experience rate of 8.2%, with divers at 9.8% and aircrew at 5.8%. Divers may be more exposed simply because pressure changes more rapidly over a short vertical distance underwater and because descent-ascent cycles occur more often, though differences in study design across the diving and aviation literature make a direct comparison difficult. A Turkish pilot survey found that 81% of those who had experienced barodontalgia placed the pain below 2,000 ft. That is a striking figure, but it comes from self-report: it points to a plausible overlap with low-altitude, pressure-changing flight segments without actually confirming the flight phase or an operational safety effect. Bruxism, occupational stress, and barodontalgia appear together in the literature, but the association is observational and says nothing about causality. General pain research backs the idea that pain can pull attention away from a task, yet no study has measured pilot performance during an actual barodontalgia episode. Taken as a whole, the evidence makes barodontalgia a biologically credible and operationally worth-watching problem, potentially preventable in principle, even if its real performance cost has not yet been quantified.
This chapter addresses the terms artificial intelligence (AI), expert systems, and machine learning (ML). We see the transition of concepts from classical programming via expert systems to ML.

Scientific model discovery requires proposing candidate models of an unknown system and designing experiments that discriminate among them. However, LLM-based approaches typically rely on in-context learning to predict outcomes and select experiments, lacking explicit model evaluation to systematically guide hypothesis search, while Bayesian approaches enable principled model comparison but are confined to a predefined candidate set which results in limited search spaces. To this end, we introduce BMD, which closes the loop between LLM-driven hypothesis generation and Bayesian experimental design. Specifically, an LLM proposes model families, while a numerical engine fits their parameters, weighs them by model evidence, and averages their predictions. Then, BMD chooses the next experimental conditions by maximizing the joint expected information gain over families and their parameters, while feeding the updated beliefs and residual diagnostics back to the LLM to guide its next proposals. Across four scientific discovery benchmarks, BMD achieves lowest final prediction error than in-context learning and LLM-based scientific agents while recovering exact functional forms more often, with ablations supporting numerical feedback and the joint objective.

This article presents a comprehensive review of technologies, tools, and applications in the field of brain-computer interfaces (BCI) and artificial intelligence (AI) for developing cognitively adaptive learning environments. Unlike prior reviews that treat BCI hardware, AI decoding models, and pedagogical deployment as separate topics, this review develops an integrated cross-layer taxonomy linking hardware constraints, AI architecture requirements, and classroom deployment conditions. Emphasis is placed on the transition from cumbersome laboratory systems to wearable hybrid solutions combining electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), as well as textile sensors that offer a favorable trade-off between neurophysiological signal quality and mobility in real-world classroom settings. The review includes a detailed analysis of modern AI architectures, transformer-based models for processing non-stationary neural signals, and Siamese neural networks implementing a few-shot learning paradigm to address the calibration problem associated with new users. It further proposes a unified state-estimation framework integrating cognitive load, attention, and affect into a single formalization for closed-loop adaptive learning systems. The review concludes with a critical analysis of fundamental barriers to scalability, signal instability, mental state privacy issues, and the risk of a neurocognitive divide arising from unequal access to technology. The authors argue that the future of neuroeducation lies in the symbiotic interaction of humans and AI, supported by unified international standards and the convergence of BCI with large language models (LLM) for predictive communication.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background: Postoperative sepsis and related infectious complications remain major causes of morbidity after abdominal surgery. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) models may support earlier risk stratification, but their generalizability and clinical readiness remain uncertain. Methods: We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and CENTRAL from inception to 10 August 2026 for studies developing, validating, or evaluating AI/ML models for postoperative sepsis, postoperative infection/surgical-site infection (SSI), anastomotic leakage, or postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) after major abdominal or general surgery. SSI, anastomotic leakage, and POPF were analyzed as distinct postoperative endpoints and were not treated as proxy definitions of clinical sepsis. Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by two reviewers, and risk of bias and applicability were assessed using PROBAST + AI. Owing to substantial clinical and methodological heterogeneity, results were synthesized narratively. The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261492111). Results: Forty-five studies were included: 11 addressed sepsis-related outcomes, including six studies with a primary sepsis-related modeled endpoint whose definitions ranged from consensus Sepsis-3 criteria to coded or SIRS-based definitions and a qSOFA-based proxy; 19 evaluated postoperative infection/SSI; eight anastomotic leakage; five POPF; and two broader postoperative complications. Performance varied according to outcome, surgical population, prediction timing, predictor availability, and validation strategy. Fifteen of 45 studies provided strict temporal, geographic/external-center, or independent-investigator evaluation of the principal model, with variable preservation of performance outside development settings. More complex ML methods did not reliably outperform conventional regression. Explicit calibration analysis was reported in 9/45 studies, decision-curve or net-benefit analysis in 7/45, and no study prospectively evaluated the impact of model-guided care on clinical outcomes. Certainty of evidence was very low for primary postoperative sepsis/septic-shock prediction, low for postoperative infection/SSI, and very low for anastomotic leakage and POPF. Conclusions: Although several AI/ML models showed promising predictive performance, the available evidence remains insufficient to support routine use of AI/ML prediction models across major abdominal surgical populations. Future studies should prioritize clearly defined clinical use cases, multicenter external validation, calibration, prospective workflow evaluation, and demonstration of actionable clinical benefit before routine implementation.

Abstract. This article presents a theoretical analysis of the impact of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on the learning activities, cognitive effort, and independent thinking of 15-year-old students in the context of Uzbekistan. The study draws on OECD PISA 2025 data and scholarly literature in behavioral sciences. According to the OECD (2026), 48.6% of students in Uzbekistan use AI chatbots for learning purposes at least once a week, while 80.6% report being taught at school how to evaluate AI-generated information. The article examines the educational implications of AI through the perspectives of cognitive offloading, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation of information. Drawing on secondary sources, the theoretical analysis suggests that AI can support learning processes, while its inappropriate use may potentially undermine independent thinking. The study emphasizes the importance of developing students' skills in responsible AI use, information verification, and independent learning. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; PISA 2025; cognitive effort; cognitive load; behavioral sciences; self-directed learning; critical thinking; Uzbekistan. Аннотация. В статье представлен теоретический анализ влияния генеративного искусственного интеллекта (ИИ) на учебную деятельность, когнитивные усилия и самостоятельное мышление 15-летних учащихся на примере Узбекистана. Исследование основано на данных PISA 2025 ОЭ. СР и научной литературе в области поведенческих наук. Согласно данным ОЭ СР (2026), 48.6% учащихся Узбекистана используют чат-боты с искусственным интеллектом в учебных целях не реже одного раза в неделю, а 80.6% отмечают, что в школе их обучают оценивать информацию, созданную ИИ. В статье рассматривается влияние ИИ на эффективность обучения с позиций когнитивной разгрузки, самостоятельного обучения и критической оценки информации. Теоретический анализ вторичных источников показывает, что ИИ может способствовать образовательному процессу, однако его ненадлежащее использование потенциально ограничивает развитие самостоятельного мышления. Обосновывается необходимость формирования у учащихся навыков осознанного использования ИИ, проверки информации и самостоятельного обучения. Ключевые слова: генеративный искусственный интеллект; PISA 2025; когнитивные усилия; когнитивная нагрузка; поведенческие науки; самостоятельное обучение; критическое мышление; Узбекистан. Annotatsiya. Ushbu maqolada generativ sun’iy intellektning (SI) 15 yoshli o‘quvchilarning o‘quv faoliyati, kognitiv sa’y-harakatlari va mustaqil fikrlashiga ta’siri O‘zbekiston misolida nazariy jihatdan tahlil qilinadi. Tadqiqot OECDning PISA 2025 ma’lumotlari va xulq-atvor fanlariga oid ilmiy adabiyotlarga asoslanadi. OECD (2026) ma’lumotlariga ko‘ra, O‘zbekistonda o‘quvchilarning 48,6 foizi haftasiga kamida bir marta o‘rganish maqsadida SI chatbotlaridan foydalanadi, 80,6 foizi esa SI yaratgan axborotni baholashni maktabda o‘rganayotganini bildirgan. Maqolada SIning ta’lim samaradorligiga ta’siri kognitiv yuklamani tashqi vositalarga o‘tkazish, mustaqil o‘rganish va axborotni tanqidiy baholash nuqtayi nazaridan yoritiladi. Ikkilamchi manbalarga asoslangan tahlil SI ta’lim jarayonini qo‘llab-quvvatlashi bilan birga, undan noto‘g‘ri foydalanish mustaqil fikrlashni cheklashi mumkinligini nazariy jihatdan ko‘rsatadi. O‘quvchilarda SIdan ongli foydalanish, axborotni tekshirish va mustaqil o‘rganish ko‘nikmalarini rivojlantirish zarurligi asoslanadi. Kalit so‘zlar: generativ sun’iy intellekt, PISA 2025, kognitiv sa'y-harakat, kognitiv yuklama, xulq-atvor fanlari, mustaqil o'rganish, tanqidiy fikrlash, O‘zbekiston.
